o: We need all prime pairs (x, y) with x ≤ y and x + y = n. Since x ≤ n/2, we only test x from 2 to n/2 and check whether both x and n−x are prime. With n up to 10⁶, primality tests must be batched: a Sieve of Eratosthenes precomputes all primes up to n in O(n log log n), after which each candidate check is O(1). Example n=10: candidates 3+7 and 5+5 are both prime pairs; 2+8 fails since 8 isn't prime. n=2 has no valid x ≥ 2 with x ≤ n−x, so the result is empty.
k: Sieve once up to n; then each pair check is O(1).
Only iterate x up to n/2 to enforce x ≤ y and avoid duplicate pairs.

a.i: Build a boolean sieve isPrime[0..n]. For each x in [2, n/2], if isPrime[x] and isPrime[n−x], record [x, n−x]. Iterating in increasing x automatically produces the required sorted output.
s: For x = 2..n//2, if both x and n−x are prime, append [x, n−x].
a.t: O(n log log n) — sieving dominates; enumeration is O(n)

a.i: Without a sieve, test each candidate x and n−x for primality by trial division up to √n. Simpler to write but slower when many candidates exist.
s: Write isPrime(v) via trial division to √v.
Enumerate x = 2..n//2, collecting pairs where both sides are prime.
a.t: O(n√n) worst case — trial division per candidate

w: Use the sieve — it's the expected answer given n up to 10⁶. Pitfalls: marking 0 and 1 non-prime, iterating x only to n/2 (otherwise duplicates like [7,3]), and n=2/n=3 edge cases yielding []. Fun follow-up: Goldbach's conjecture guarantees pairs exist for even n ≥ 4.
